researchNotes.title: Old channels and younger stream gravels
researchNotes.text: USGS PP610 distinguishes buried Tertiary auriferous gravels from younger stream placers on California’s western Sierra slope, alongside major lode districts. The placer province spans numerous districts/counties; old channels may be buried, worked out or inaccessible.

researchNotes.locator: Printed p. 55, Mother Lode vein mineralogy
researchNotes.title: Mother Lode quartz and sulfides
researchNotes.text: PP610 describes Mother Lode ore as quartz veins and mineralized country rock along reverse-fault zones. Milky, locally ribboned quartz commonly accompanies small amounts of sulfides, mainly pyrite. This is a regional lode association; quartz or pyrite alone does not establish placer gold.

history.title: The Pierce discovery
history.text: IGS records a gold discovery near Pierce in 1860. That is an important mining-development date, but it is not presented here as proof that no earlier gold occurrence was known.

overview.text: The Pierce-area gold discovery in 1860 is a landmark in Idaho’s mining history. Idaho Geological Survey’s district publications and mine-history records offer a route into that history, alongside information on the geological settings and hazards of inactive workings.

discovery.label: Initial discovery in the survey account

history.title: Alaska and the Klondike
history.text: The Klondike goldfields were in Canada’s Yukon. Skagway and Dyea served as Alaska gateways to them, while the later Nome rush brought miners to Alaska’s own goldfields. NPS also documents how these migrations disrupted Alaska Native trading relationships.

overview.text: Alaska’s gold occurs in both bedrock deposits and placer gravels. The state geological survey describes gold mining in the Interior and Southeast, alongside placer operations. discovery.label: Early documented gold report

history.title: The nineteenth-century placer era
history.text: The 1972 USGS compilation identifies 1858–1880 as Arizona’s most productive placer-mining era, particularly in the southwestern and central parts of the state. Its historical districts are a research guide, not a list of currently open collecting parcels.

places.title: Lynx Creek drainage
places.text: The USGS catalog treats Lynx Creek drainage as a historical placer district in Yavapai County. The district description concerns gold occurrence and past mining; permission for a specific parcel needs separate confirmation.

places.text: A separate Yavapai County district in the USGS placer catalog. Use its historical geology as a starting point for research, with land ownership and claim status checked independently.

accessNotes.title: Start with ownership and designated areas
accessNotes.text: AZGS advises prospectors to respect ownership and designated-land restrictions. Its lode and placer reports document geology and historical workings; they do not grant permission to enter a property or work a mining claim.
accessNotes.locator: Gold prospecting publications and ownership guidance

overview.text: Arizona has both lode and placer gold. The USGS placer survey relates much of the placer gold to small quartz veinlets in neighboring mountain bedrock; erosion released the gold into gravels. Drywashers, sluices and occasional larger dredging operations formed part of its mining history.
overview.locator: Abstract, printed p. 1 / PDF p. 8

discovery.label: Early recorded placer mining
discovery.text: USGS dates an early Quijotoa Mountains placer-mining account to 1774, involving Indigenous miners under Manuel Lopez’s direction. This is a mining-history record, not proof of when gold was first known in present-day Arizona.
discovery.locator: History of Placer Mining in Arizona, printed p. 1 / PDF p. 8

researchNotes.text: Lynx Creek Gold Pan Day Use Area lists year-round use with four seasonal daily-hour schedules. Year-round opening does not mean dependable water or a statewide best month.

facts.label: Estimated historical placer gold
facts.definition: Statewide estimated placer production in the 1994 compilation. This excludes lode gold and is an estimate rather than a complete ledger: early production is poorly documented, and some district totals remain unknown. It does not describe current production or reserves.

history.text: The bureau dates the discovery of large Old Placers deposits in the Ortiz Mountains, Santa Fe County, to 1828. It separately reports placer mining along the northern Rio Grande in the 1600s, so the rush date is not presented as the state’s first discovery.
history.title: The Ortiz Mountains rush

history.text: Weathering releases gold from lode sources; water and gravity concentrate it in gravels. The bureau describes gold near bedrock, fractures and clay or caliche layers, including narrow pay streaks. These processes explain historical deposits without guaranteeing recoverable gold at any particular stream.
history.title: From lodes to gravels

places.text: The Old Placers district lies in Santa Fe County around the Ortiz Mountains. The bureau records placer deposits on the southern and eastern flanks. This is a historical district reference; present access and permission are unverified.
places.locator: Opening history paragraphs
places.title: Old Placers · Ortiz Mountains

places.text: The Hillsboro or Las Animas district lies in the Animas Mountains, Sierra County. The bureau describes past production from polymetallic veins and placer gold, with mineralization tied to the Copper Flat volcanic and intrusive complex. Its district history dates the Gold Dust prospecting settlement to 1881. Present prospecting access is unverified.
places.locator: Summary; Location and Mining History; Local Geology
places.title: Hillsboro · Animas Mountains

overview.text: New Mexico’s gold history includes both placer deposits and lode sources. The state geological bureau describes placers in stream gravels, terraces, alluvial fans and weathered material over lodes. The Ortiz Mountains rush of 1828 was a landmark, while earlier northern Rio Grande mining is reported.
overview.locator: Opening history and placer geology paragraphs

discovery.label: Earliest reported placer mining
discovery.text: New Mexico’s geological bureau records placer mining along the northern Rio Grande in the 1600s. The 1828 discovery of large Ortiz Mountains placers began a later rush; it is not substituted for the earlier mining record.

researchNotes.locator: Placer geology; production; minerals; water limitations; revised April 9, 2025
researchNotes.title: Fans, terraces and river-bar placers
researchNotes.text: McLemore estimates 662,000 ounces of New Mexico placer gold for 1828–1991. Four districts exceed 100,000 ounces each: Elizabethtown–Baldy, Hillsboro, Old Placers and New Placers. Deposits include fans, terraces, river bars and residual material over lodes; this is historical placer output, not all gold or a remaining reserve.

researchNotes.locator: Placer geology; production; minerals; water limitations; revised April 9, 2025
researchNotes.title: Minerals and layers found with placer gold
researchNotes.text: The Bureau lists quartz, magnetite, ilmenite, amphiboles, pyroxenes, pyrite, zircon, garnet and rutile with native gold/electrum. Pay streaks may sit on bedrock or clay/caliche lenses. These associations help interpret a deposit but do not demonstrate gold in a particular pan.

researchNotes.locator: Placer geology; production; minerals; water limitations; revised April 9, 2025
researchNotes.title: Water availability matters
researchNotes.text: The Bureau identifies lack of water as a historical constraint in many districts. It does not supply a statewide best-month schedule; verify local water and legal access before choosing wet processing.

history.title: Mercur and changing recovery methods
history.text: UGS describes an initially unsuccessful placer effort at Mercur, followed by gold-bearing ores that were difficult to process. Successful cyanide recovery in 1889 changed the district’s mining prospects.

places.title: Bingham Canyon
places.text: UGS describes Bingham’s historic placers as Utah’s largest and most productive, while noting that open-pit mining has altered the original topography. Historical placer descriptions do not imply a remaining recreational site.
places.locator: Early Discoveries; Oquirrh Mountains, Bingham Canyon

places.title: Abajo Mountains
places.text: UGS reports historical placer occurrences along Johnson and Recapture Creeks. This is occurrence evidence only; present land ownership, claims and permitted activities still need site-specific research.
places.locator: Where are Utah’s gold placers? Item 1

places.title: Gold Hill · Tooele County
places.text: UGS identifies Gold Hill as the location of the reported 1858 discovery by westbound travelers.
places.locator: Early Discoveries, opening paragraphs

overview.text: Utah’s gold history includes both placer and lode deposits, with lode mining proving more economical. UGS describes much of the state’s placer gold as very fine grained, so a recorded occurrence should not be read as a promise of easy recovery.
overview.locator: Lode and Placer Deposits; What is a placer?

discovery.label: First reported discovery in the survey account
discovery.text: Utah Geological Survey dates the reported discovery at Gold Hill, Tooele County, to 1858. Its history separately dates the Bingham Canyon placer find to 1864.

researchNotes.locator: Lode and Placer Deposits; Utah’s Gold Placers; Bluff excitement; recreational rules
researchNotes.title: The Bluff gold excitement
researchNotes.text: UGS recounts the 1892–93 Bluff excitement, when exaggerated San Juan River placer stories attracted prospectors who found fine gold difficult to recover. The episode is useful evidence against treating a rush story as a yield forecast.

overview.text: New Hampshire has documented gold in bedrock veins and stream gravels. NHDES describes small quantities and a short-lived nineteenth-century mining rush around Lyman and Bath. The Ammonoosuc district is a useful place to begin geological reading; it is not a map of places where you have permission to prospect.

history.title: Lyman and Bath’s short-lived gold rush
history.text: NHDES dates the Lyman discovery that sparked a local rush to 1864. Mines near Bath supplied two mills, but the operations were short-lived. This is a regional history date, not a verified first discovery for the whole state.

places.title: Ammonoosuc gold district · historical reference
places.text: The official fact sheet identifies a district centered on Lyman, Monroe and Bath, with gold in quartz veins and associated sulfide minerals. A historic district name does not establish current ownership, permission or an expected yield.
places.locator: Fact sheet p. 2

accessNotes.title: Hand panning and larger equipment follow different rules
accessNotes.text: NHDES’s 2020 guidance calls for landowner permission, prohibits shoveling into streambeds or banks for hand panning, and describes permits for dredging or similar work. Check current NHDES requirements and the relevant land manager before choosing equipment.
accessNotes.locator: Fact sheet p. 2 · dated guidance, reconfirm before a trip

mines.title: Dodge Gold Mine
mines.text: Hoskins places Dodge Gold Mine on the old Hall farm in Lyman. Ross’s field study adds a later chapter: intermittent work and a cyanide mill, with the mine already abandoned when he visited in summer 1915. Its exact modern entrance remains unresolved.
mines.dates: Worked before 1903; abandoned by Ross’s summer-1915 visit. Exact opening and final closing dates unresolved.

location.description: Old Hall farm, Lyman; precise workings not reconciled.

mines.locator: Lyman Master Plan, printed page 10; NHDES GEO-1 historical summary

historyNotes.title: The Hall family connection
historyNotes.text: Hoskins identifies the site with the farm settled by Abram Hall and Sarah Floyd. He says Abram lived there until his death in 1855, and that Abram Jr. later remained on the home place. These are farm-family details, not evidence that either man operated the gold mine.
historyNotes.locator: Printed p. 102 (PDF p. 128), Abram Hall biography

historyNotes.title: 1903 · mining remembered
historyNotes.text: Hoskins describes earlier extensive work at Dodge, and a separate nearby Tunnel Mine then being worked. His monetary and ore-quality claims are not independently verified here and are not used as production statistics.

historyNotes.title: The landscape today
historyNotes.text: Ammonoosuc Conservation Trust identifies the former Dodge Mine within its account of the Godfrey Memorial Conservation Area and says forest has reclaimed the site. The account does not establish permission to prospect or supply a mine-entrance coordinate.

historyNotes.title: A historical map connection
historyNotes.text: The 1957 USGS statewide mineral map lists Dodge alongside Allen, Atwood and Lisbon in Grafton County locality group 49. The grouped symbol and 1:500,000 scale are too broad to identify a precise entrance.

historyNotes.title: Summer 1915 · already abandoned
historyNotes.text: Ross reports a cyanide mill erected after Hitchcock’s 1878 account and intermittent later work. On his summer-1915 visit, Dodge was abandoned. This establishes its condition at that visit, not the exact date it closed.

historyNotes.title: A closer geological map
historyNotes.text: Ross includes a district geological map and structural sections. They help place the workings in their geological setting; no modern entrance coordinate has been derived from them here.

mines.text: NHDES reports a small gold shipment to the mint from a Diamond Ledge Mine in Ossipee. Similar names also occur in mineral-locality indexes. A reliable match between this account and a mine coordinate has not yet been established.

location.description: Ossipee in the NHDES account; exact mine identity unresolved.

historyNotes.text: The 1957 USGS map separately lists White Diamond gold mine as Carroll County locality 6, referring to Meyers (1941). That name is a lead to compare with the NHDES Diamond Ledge account; the two records have not been proven to describe the same working.

historyNotes.text: Allison’s Dublin history names a Diamond Ledge Gold Mine Company and connects it to Gold Mine Road there. That is a separate town and account, not evidence locating the Ossipee working.

mines.text: A separate tunnel intended to reach the Dodge veins at depth. Ross describes it as about 900 feet long and says it failed to reach its intended target. It is retained as a distinct historical working, without an invented entrance point.
mines.dates: Worked in Hoskins’s 1903 account; already abandoned in Ross’s 1914–1915 field study.

overview.text: Vermont’s gold history includes quartz-vein workings and stream placers around Bridgewater and Plymouth. Historical geological accounts describe uneven deposits and unreliable profit claims. For a practical starting point, Vermont State Parks publishes a specific hand-panning opportunity at Camp Plymouth, with clear equipment limits.

history.title: Two kinds of deposits, two different histories
history.text: E. L. Perry’s 1929 account distinguishes quartz veins from placer deposits. It dates a Bridgewater vein discovery to 1851 and reports Plymouth placer activity by about 1855. These district dates are not presented as Vermont’s first gold discovery.

history.title: Old production claims need careful handling
history.text: The same account warns that Plymouth’s reported historical dollar totals are unreliable. They are not converted here into a statewide production total or a prediction of what a visitor can find today.

accessNotes.title: State-park hand tools and streambed limits
accessNotes.text: Vermont State Parks allows traditional hand panning with small hand tools. Its rules exclude sluices, rocker boxes and powered or moving equipment, and limit material removal to the streambed rather than banks. The same page says gold panning is not allowed in state wildlife management areas.
accessNotes.locator: Gold Panning rules

accessNotes.title: Private-land sluicing needs separate approval
accessNotes.text: The Rivers Program’s May 2023 guidance requires landowner permission for private-land panning and both owner permission and state approval for sluicing on private land. It states that suction dredges for mineral prospecting in streams are prohibited. Ask the Rivers Program about current requirements for your proposed activity.
accessNotes.locator: PDF p. 1; contact details on p. 2

mines.title: Rooks Mine / Fox Mine
mines.text: A quartz-vein gold working near Plymouth, also known as Fox Mine. MRDS records production in 1883–1887. Later accounts disagree about when Henry Fox acquired it: Beth R. Smith gives a late-1887 auction, while State Parks says 1889. Neither establishes uninterrupted commercial production through his death in 1919.
mines.dates: 1883–1887 production in MRDS; Fox purchase dated 1887 or 1889 in different accounts; later searching through 1919.

location.description: Plymouth, Windsor County; Reading Pond / Buffalo Brook area

mines.locator: MRDS DEP_ID 10081526; State Parks history; Perry 1929 excerpt, PDF pages 10–11

historyNotes.title: 1903 · a geologist visits
historyNotes.text: G. O. Smith visited the old Rooks workings near Tyson. He could not inspect the openings and found little encouraging material on the dumps. His report describes an ambitious operation with no apparent profit.

historyNotes.title: 1929 · the hillside workings
historyNotes.text: Perry describes a brook-level adit and mill ruins, with upper shaft workings about 170 feet higher. He identifies native gold but describes its distribution as too irregular and low-grade for profitable mining. These are historical observations, not present conditions.

historyNotes.title: Henry Fox · two purchase dates
historyNotes.text: Beth R. Smith recounts Fox’s lawsuit for unpaid salary and a sheriff’s sale at Ludlow, placing his ownership in late 1887. State Parks instead gives 1889. The deed or court record is still needed to reconcile them.

mines.title: Taggart vein / Bridgewater Gold Mines
mines.text: Worked intermittently around 1859 west of Bridgewater Center. Historical accounts describe mills and claimed gold returns, but a sampled ore assay reported no gold. The GIS commodity fields emphasize lead and copper. This is evidence of gold-seeking activity, with disputed gold results.
mines.dates: Intermittent work around 1859; full operating span unresolved.

historyNotes.title: 1859 onward · the Thompson farm vein
historyNotes.text: Smith places the Taggart vein on the old Thompson farm, one mile west of Bridgewater Center, with intermittent work beginning in 1859 and openings along a small stream gulch.

historyNotes.title: An assay that did not confirm the gold claims
historyNotes.text: A sample from quartz and galena beside an opening returned no gold in the Survey laboratory, despite earlier claimed returns. One sample does not prove every part of the vein is gold-free; it does explain why the gold results remain disputed.

historyNotes.title: Separate nearby projects

overview.text: Massachusetts is worth approaching with a geological map rather than a promise of a gold-bearing stream. USGS’s statewide surficial mapping distinguishes glacial till, meltwater deposits and younger river sediments. Those maps help explain the ground beneath a stream, but do not show that gold occurs there. No specific Massachusetts placer site has been verified in this first research pass.

history.title: Reported deposits are not the same as proven gold
history.text: Laurence La Forge’s 1932 Boston-area report records gold, copper and lead reports prompted by sulfide veins in quarries, but says valuable recoveries there were not established. This historical assessment concerns the Boston area; it does not prove that Massachusetts has no gold.

history.title: A useful map for reading the landscape
history.text: The statewide USGS compilation covers 189 quadrangles at 1:24,000 scale and distinguishes bedrock exposure, glacial deposits and postglacial sediments. Use it as a geology research aid, not a prospecting-access map.

accessNotes.title: Check the land manager before collecting
accessNotes.text: For DCR parks and forests, begin with DCR’s current Parks and Recreation rules and ask the park manager about your exact collecting activity. The agency separately lists draft rules under review; a draft or geological map does not establish permission. No public hand-panning site is verified here yet.

researchNotes.title: Detailed surficial geology maps
researchNotes.text: USGS SIM3402 maps till, glacial stratified deposits and postglacial sediments across 189 quadrangles at 1:24,000, with downloadable sheets and geodatabases. Its material classes support geological interpretation; they are not gold-occurrence measurements.

overview.text: Connecticut’s official mine inventory is a good starting point for researching historical mineral workings. Its technical report describes historical gold mining only as possible, while documenting many other commodities. This first pass has not verified a Connecticut placer-gold destination or a statewide gold-production figure. A mine symbol on a map should not be read as a gold find or visitor access.

history.title: A mining inventory, not a gold-mine count
history.text: The 2022 version 1.01 inventory documents 1,070 bedrock mining sites across many commodities, including mines and quarries of different activity statuses. That total is deliberately excluded from the gold statistics cards: it is not a count of gold mines.

accessNotes.title: State-land collecting is restricted
accessNotes.text: Connecticut DEEP says collecting rocks and minerals on state land is not allowed without authorization. Scientific or educational collecting may be considered through written application. Its mining database also warns that many listed sites are private property and that a mapped site grants no visiting permission.

researchNotes.text: Connecticut DEEP’s collecting guidance quotes rules against removing earth or rock material on department lands except as authorized. Written scientific or educational collecting permission can be requested; a mineral-club listing does not itself authorize collecting.

overview.text: Rhode Island has historical prospects and small mines named for gold in USGS’s 1971 bedrock-geology report. The author emphasizes how little was known about when some deposits were worked, the extent of mining or even the commodity sought. Treat these as historical research leads, not established modern panning destinations.

history.title: What an old gold-mine name can tell us
history.text: Quinn’s report preserves names such as Durfee Hill, Snake Den and Bald Hill, while warning that mining records are sparse. The names alone do not provide reliable production totals, workable deposits or permission to collect.

overview.text: New York’s rich mining history does not imply a comparable history of producing gold mines. The State Museum’s historical overview says colonial searches did not find gold and silver in economic quantities. No individual historic gold mine has been verified for this guide yet; that is a research gap, not proof that gold is absent.

researchNotes.title: New York’s reserved gold and silver rights
researchNotes.text: New York Public Lands Law §81 reserves gold and silver deposits to the state, including deposits on private land, and addresses permission to explore state land. It does not settle how incidental recreational flakes are treated. Ask the responsible state agencies before collecting; private landowner permission alone does not resolve the mineral-rights question.

overview.text: Dahlonega anchors North Georgia’s gold-mining history. Georgia DNR describes a gold rush into the Cherokee Nation before the California rush. Today, a managed panning lesson offers a way to practice without treating historical mining districts as open-access sites.

overview.text: Colorado’s gold deposits are geologically diverse. Stream placers near Denver helped spark the nineteenth-century rush, while districts such as Central City, Cripple Creek and Telluride developed substantial bedrock mining. Historic occurrence, modern production and recreational access need to be considered separately.

overview.text: Wyoming’s gold occurs in primary bedrock deposits and in placers formed by weathering and erosion. WSGS associates primary deposits with Precambrian mountain uplifts and some younger volcanic and intrusive rocks. South Pass–Atlantic City is a central part of the state’s mining history.
overview.locator: Gold geology; History

history.title: The 1867 Carissa rush
history.text: WSGS links Wyoming’s first major gold rush to the 1867 discovery of bedrock gold in the Carissa lode. The earlier Sweetwater placer reports are a different historical milestone, not the start of that rush.

places.title: South Pass–Atlantic City
places.text: WSGS identifies this as Wyoming’s foremost early mining district. Its historic towns and lode records provide context for the gold rush; access to individual workings needs separate verification.
places.locator: History; mining districts

places.title: Douglas Creek district

discovery.label: Early reported placer gold

researchNotes.title: Why there is no reliable statewide total
researchNotes.text: WSGS links the 1867 rush to the Carissa lode and states that total Wyoming production is unknown because early records were not kept. Its Carissa estimate of 50,000–180,000 ounces before 1911 is mine-specific and must not become a statewide total.

overview.text: Michigan’s gold story includes historic bedrock mining around Ishpeming and small placer occurrences in glacial deposits. The state’s older Survey compilation explains that transported gold in Lower Peninsula drift does not establish a nearby bedrock gold source.

researchNotes.text: Michigan DNR’s guidance applies where the state owns both surface and mineral rights. Power sluicing is prohibited, and closed habitats include designated trout streams, natural rivers and natural areas, and Great Lakes shores and bottomlands. Sluicing requires EGLE permitting. Confirm the permits for your exact hand-panning activity with DNR and EGLE before collecting.

overview.text: Minnesota’s gold history includes quartz-hosted discoveries near Lake Vermilion and Rainy Lake. DNR distinguishes possible bedrock gold from placer exploration: glacial sediments can carry gold grains, but the agency reports no commercial placer-gold discovery in the state.

history.text: A Lake Vermilion gold rush took place in 1865–66. Rainy Lake’s Little American Island became another gold-mining center after an 1893 discovery.

overview.text: Montana’s gold history spans placer gravels and hard-rock deposits. Bannack and Alder Gulch became major early rush centers. The state geological bureau describes varied bedrock sources and a landscape repeatedly shaped by glaciation, erosion and stream transport.

history.title: The Bannack rush
history.text: Montana FWP dates Bannack’s first major strike to July 28, 1862. The discovery triggered a rush, and Bannack became the first territorial capital.

history.title: Alder Gulch and changing methods
history.text: The Heritage Commission dates the Alder Gulch discovery to May 26, 1863. Hand-worked gravels later gave way to hydraulic mining in 1867 and floating dredges from 1898 to 1922, leaving extensive tailings and ponds.

history.title: Different rocks, reworked gravels
history.text: MBMG places Montana’s placers in drainages of ancient crystalline rocks, Belt sedimentary rocks and younger rocks near granitic intrusions. Glaciers, outwash, debris flows and floods repeatedly reworked deposits; a nearby known lode is not always the source.

places.title: Bannack · Grasshopper Creek

places.title: Alder Gulch · Virginia City and Nevada City

overview.text: South Dakota’s gold story centers on the Black Hills. USGS describes Homestake’s gold in ancient iron-formation and other deposits in the Deadwood Formation. The rush after the 1874 expedition also brought miners onto treaty-protected Sioux reservation lands, making Indigenous history part of the mining story.

facts.label: Historical gold production
facts.definition: USGS cumulative statewide output includes lode, placer and byproduct gold. Early figures include estimates; this is historical production, not remaining reserves.

history.text: The National Park Service describes miners entering the Black Hills after the 1874 expedition confirmed gold. The 1868 Fort Laramie Treaty required the United States to keep settlers out of the Sioux reservation. Grant’s late-1875 decision to stop removing miners accompanied policies that escalated conflict.

history.text: USGS’s 1974 account distinguishes ancient ore bodies at Homestake from later hydrothermal replacement deposits in the Cambrian Deadwood Formation. At Homestake, ore occurs in the iron-rich Homestake Formation and is concentrated in structures produced by folding. This is a historical geological account.

history.text: South Dakota’s regulatory history dates Homestake’s last mined gold ore to December 14, 2001. Milling continued until the last ore was processed on January 18, 2002, and the mill shut down on February 13. Mining and milling therefore have different closure dates.

researchNotes.title: Quartz veins and their host rocks
researchNotes.text: McCaskey’s 1908 reconnaissance places Alabama gold districts in east-central metamorphic and crystalline rocks. It records quartz veins in granite, gneiss, schist and slate; at Pinetuckey, gold-bearing schist beside a vein contains garnets. This is a historical, site-specific association rather than a statewide indicator recipe.

overview.text: Arkansas’s gold record includes historical investigations and small mineral occurrences. The state Geological Survey describes sparse gold and silver in vein material associated with igneous dikes near Hot Springs.
overview.locator: Arkansas historical investigations paragraph: 1923 Hot Springs findings

history.title: The Ouachita investigation
history.text: Gold reports in the early 1880s prompted the Arkansas Geological Survey’s inquiry into the Ouachita Mountains, published in its 1888 annual report.
history.locator: Historical investigations paragraph: early 1880s and Annual Report 1888, Volume I

places.title: Hot Springs, Garland County
places.text: The Survey summarizes 1923 USGS findings of sparse gold and silver in vein material near Hot Springs, Garland County. The association was with igneous dikes.
places.locator: Historical investigations paragraph: 1923 USGS Hot Springs, Garland County

overview.text: Southern Louisiana’s Mississippi River delta provides a sedimentary geology background. At Jean Lafitte, NPS describes young river and delta deposits of sand, silt, and clay. A gold-bearing locality remains unverified in this review.
overview.locator: Geologic Setting; final sentence states this research packet’s verification status, not a claim of gold absence

overview.text: Mississippi’s Office of Geology describes minute gold particles transported with sediments from distant source rocks. Its 1994 review also reports detectable gold in subsurface igneous-rock samples from the Jackson Dome.
overview.locator: Printed/PDF p. 1: natural gold, transported particles and Jackson Dome drill-hole samples

history.title: A long history of gold reports
history.text: The 1994 review revisits Lewis Harper’s 1857 account of repeated submissions of pyrite mistaken for gold. Historical interest and rumors do not establish a gold deposit.
history.locator: Printed/PDF p. 2: Harper 1857 and mistaken mineral identifications

places.title: Jackson Dome—subsurface evidence
places.text: The 1994 review cites detectable gold in drill-hole samples of hydrothermally altered igneous rock from the Jackson Dome. This subsurface result does not identify a surface panning site.
places.locator: Printed/PDF p. 1: Saunders 1993 drill-hole samples

researchNotes.locator: 1997–1998 soil/sediment survey; USGS OFR2004-1001 datasets; atlas links
researchNotes.title: Soil and sediment geochemistry
researchNotes.text: MDEQ provides Mississippi’s statewide 1997–1998 soil/sediment geochemical survey through USGS OFR2004-1001 and extracted PDF/Excel datasets. Consult sampling methods and detection limits; a geochemical anomaly alone is not a recoverable gold placer.

researchNotes.locator: Mineral identifications; iron-rich minerals; lithic map links
researchNotes.title: Iron-rich nodules are not gold evidence
researchNotes.text: MDEQ’s lithic guide describes siderite, goethite and limonite among Mississippi materials. These iron-rich nodules and colors should not be treated as positive gold indicators without independent gold evidence.

overview.text: Oklahoma’s gold-related records include literature reports of trace gold in the Wichita Mountains. USGS’s 2023 mapping announcement lists those reports within a broader mineral inventory.
overview.locator: Opening project description: Wichita Mountains; trace gold and silver reported in literature

history.title: The Wichita Mountains gold rush
history.text: Oklahoma Geological Survey’s 2014 newsletter describes a Wichita Mountains geology-trail exhibit about the 1901–1907 gold rush. It notes that a 1904 USGS investigation found no gold in the mines it sampled.
history.locator: Printed/PDF p. 4, Figure 4 caption; p. 3 identifies Burford Lake trail in Wichita Mountains refuge

places.title: Wichita Mountains
places.text: USGS reports that trace gold and silver have been described in literature concerning the Wichita Mountains. The announcement is a report of prior literature, not confirmation of a visitor prospecting site.
places.locator: Opening project description: literature-reported trace gold and silver

accessNotes.title: Wichita Mountains Wildlife Refuge
accessNotes.text: Wichita Mountains Wildlife Refuge’s visitor rules prohibit ordinary collection of rocks and minerals and the use of metal detectors. Its caves, tunnels, and mines are closed to entry. Special-use collection permits do not provide general visitor permission.
accessNotes.locator: General Regulations: collection prohibition, metal detectors, mines/caves closure, and special-use collection permit inspection

researchNotes.locator: Prohibited activities; collection and metal detectors
researchNotes.title: Wichita Mountains refuge restrictions
researchNotes.text: Wichita Mountains Wildlife Refuge prohibits collecting rocks and minerals and prohibits metal detectors and treasure/artifact searching. Historical gold reports in the Wichita Mountains do not override this refuge rule.

overview.text: Texas has a modest recorded gold history. Historical surveys describe gold in the Llano uplift and West Texas; the state’s reported production largely came alongside silver and copper mining. The records below describe geology and historical workings, with sources for further reading.
overview.locator: Circular 5, PDF p. 1; Handbook of Texas, opening production account

facts.label: Reported historical gold output
facts.definition: The Handbook of Texas reports this historical total from the Presidio, Hazel and Heath mines, chiefly as a silver- and copper-mining byproduct. This is a dated historical account, not an all-time total or a modern panning yield.
facts.locator: Opening production account

facts.label: Gold-bearing inventory records
facts.definition: Entries in the Bureau’s Gold map layer, including occurrences, prospects and historical producers. Some mine names appear more than once. This counts database records, not unique mines or operations active today.
facts.locator: Layer 7; count of returned OBJECTID records

history.title: A historical mineral inventory
history.text: The 1927 inventory notes that small amounts of gold had been produced in Texas. Its production statements describe that historical period.
history.locator: GOLD section, printed/PDF p. 14: Uses and past production

history.title: Gold alongside silver and copper
history.text: The Handbook identifies Presidio and Hazel in West Texas and Heath in the Llano district as the principal historical producers. It records Presidio’s closure in September 1942; that is a historical milestone, not a statement about present-day operations.

places.title: Central Texas quartz-vein counties
places.text: The 1927 inventory lists gold in quartz veins in Blanco, Burnet, Gillespie, and Mason counties. These are historical mineral-occurrence records.
places.locator: GOLD section, printed/PDF p. 14: named quartz-vein counties

places.title: Brewster County
places.text: The same 1927 inventory records small quantities of gold with mercury ores in Brewster County. This ore association does not establish recreational collecting access.
places.locator: GOLD section, printed/PDF p. 14: mercury ores, Brewster County

places.title: Llano River drainage
places.text: The 1932 geological account discusses the Llano River drainage as a setting for placer investigation. It distinguishes geological possibilities from a demonstrated profitable deposit. A named river does not establish a place open to collecting.
places.locator: PDF pp. 3–4, Llano Uplift of Central Texas

places.title: Sandy Creek drainage
places.text: Baker’s 1932 report discusses Sandy Creek and its tributaries in relation to gold-bearing rocks and sediment concentration. This is historical geological context; present-day yield and collecting arrangements are not established here.
places.locator: PDF pp. 3–4, Llano Uplift of Central Texas

places.title: Heath Mine · Llano County
places.text: The Bureau’s Gold layer lists Heath as a past producer in Llano County. The inventory’s undated status does not establish its current condition or access.
places.locator: Layer 7, OBJECTID 13

accessNotes.title: Check park rules before collecting
accessNotes.text: TPWD’s published rules restrict disturbing or removing geological materials in state parks except by director-issued permit. Metal detectors also require authorization. Check the current park rules and contact staff before planning any collecting activity.

accessNotes.title: State mineral permissions
accessNotes.text: The General Land Office provides prospect-permit and hard-mineral lease procedures. Arrangements depend on the mineral and land category. A geological inventory or public access to a site does not itself provide mineral permission.
accessNotes.locator: Opening guidance; Prospecting; Hard Mineral Leasing

researchNotes.locator: PDF p. 1, Llano Uplift of Central Texas
researchNotes.title: Llano’s veinlets and host rocks
researchNotes.text: Baker’s 1932 Llano account places gold in quartz veinlets/stringers in metamorphic schist, quartzite, phyllite, slate and marble. It separately cautions that conspicuous broad milky-white quartz veins in the region were not known to contain gold. Do not equate every quartz vein with an auriferous source.

overview.text: Illinois’ historical gold literature includes scattered sediment reports and a reported small bedrock occurrence. The state geological survey’s 1968 compilation is explicitly preliminary: observed specimens, reported finds and speculative targets have different levels of support.
overview.locator: Foreword; printed pp. 2–5 and Table 2, p. 20

history.text: The compilation discusses gold transported from Canada by glaciers and reworked into outwash and younger alluvium. Its proposed concentration targets were hypotheses; a mapped glacial landform alone does not establish a gold occurrence.
history.title: Glacial transport as a historical interpretation

places.text: The 1968 compilation says F. W. DeWolf examined gravel from near Channahon and reported gold, without stating an amount. The entry is based on survey correspondence and supplies no precise sampling location.
places.locator: Table 2, printed p. 20, item 4 / PDF p. 26
places.title: Channahon area

places.text: The compilation cites the survey’s 1926 Dixon quadrangle report for gold reported panned from Rock River gravel. This is a historical regional account.
places.locator: Table 2, printed p. 20, item 7 / PDF p. 26
places.title: Rock River

overview.text: Iowa’s survey describes small amounts of gold transported in glacial sediment from Minnesota and Canada. Rivers cutting those deposits can rework grains and flakes into sand and gravel. The survey’s 1999 account identifies several historical stream reports.
overview.locator: EM-16, p. 1, Iowa-specific geology and waterway paragraph

history.text: The survey recounts an 1853 report by Eldora innkeeper John Ellsworth of gold on his Iowa River farm. News drew a local rush to the Eldora area.
history.title: Eldora’s nineteenth-century gold excitement

places.text: The 1999 survey account lists historical gold reports along the Iowa River near Eldora and Steamboat Rock in Hardin County.
places.locator: EM-16, p. 1, historic waterway list
places.title: Iowa River: Eldora–Steamboat Rock

places.text: The same account describes a small placer operation that recovered gold from Big Sioux River gravels at Klondike in Lyon County in the early 1900s.
places.locator: EM-16, p. 1, Big Sioux River and Klondike sentence
places.title: Big Sioux River: Klondike area

researchNotes.locator: EM16, January 1999, one page; glacial provenance; small grains/flakes; Klondike history
researchNotes.title: Eldora and Iowa’s Klondike
researchNotes.text: The Iowa survey identifies a small early-1900s placer operation near Klondike on the Big Sioux River as its only known commercial gold venture. Its 1853 Eldora rush account credits innkeeper John Ellsworth. Neither account supplies a statewide production total.

overview.text: Gold claims in western Kansas shales prompted a USGS investigation published in 1902. Testing found very small quantities of gold in some samples, with results that were not always reproduced. These are findings from a defined historical shale study.
overview.locator: Bulletin 202, printed pp. 18–19, Summary and Conclusions

history.text: USGS collected shale from Ellis and Rush counties, chiefly along the Smoky Hill River, including pits and quarries associated with contemporary gold-mill claims. Repeated assays varied, and the report explicitly limited its conclusions to the tested material.
history.title: Testing western Kansas shale claims

places.text: The 1902 investigation sampled Benton shale exposures in Ellis and Rush counties along the Smoky Hill River. Some assays detected very small amounts of gold; the locality is a historical rock-sampling study area.
places.locator: Bulletin 202, printed pp. 18–19
places.title: Smoky Hill shale study area

overview.text: Missouri’s gold research trail includes Garland Carr Broadhead’s nineteenth-century article about drift formation and gold. The state geological survey preserves its bibliographic record; the article’s occurrence details await inspection of the original.
overview.locator: Catalogue item 352, title, author and publication fields

history.text: The agency catalogue identifies Broadhead’s article in the February 1876 American Journal of Science, following an 1875 publication. This establishes a historical research reference, without verifying its reported gold findings.
history.locator: Catalogue item 352, title and American Journal of Science publication field
history.title: A documented nineteenth-century research reference

history.text: The survey’s 2020 fact sheet describes northern Missouri’s Glacial Till Plains as quartz-rich sand and varied gravel, including chert, limestone, quartzite, granite and mafic rocks, commonly held in a clay matrix. This is regional sediment geology.
history.locator: PUB2903, Composition of Sand and Gravel: Glacial Till Plains of northern Missouri
history.title: Northern Missouri’s glacial sediment background

researchNotes.locator: Common Names; pyrite and magnetite; mineral identification
researchNotes.title: Pyrite, magnetite and hematite
researchNotes.text: Missouri DNR’s iron guide identifies pyrite as fool’s gold and distinguishes magnetite from hematite. These are useful identification references, but their presence alone does not demonstrate a Missouri gold placer.

overview.text: A USGS compilation published in 1917 records placer gold in Nebraska’s Platte River sands and glacial drift. Its brief entry is a historical regional observation, without specific sampling sites or a statewide production total.
overview.locator: Bulletin 624, Nebraska, printed p. 188, Gold (placer)

history.text: The Nebraska survey’s 2023 Leshara sheet maps Platte River alluvium with sand, silt and clay, alongside windblown loess over older alluvium and glacial sediment. The map describes sediment history; it does not document gold at Leshara.
history.locator: Sheet 1, Description of Mapping Units: Qap1–Qap3 and Qp
history.title: Platte River sediment context

places.text: The 1917 USGS Nebraska entry names Platte River sands as a placer-gold occurrence. It identifies a broad river region, with no particular river reach or recovery estimate.
places.locator: Bulletin 624, Nebraska, printed p. 188, Gold (placer)
places.title: Platte River: historical regional record

overview.text: North Dakota’s survey describes gold in preglacial river gravel near Fort Ransom and in glacial Lake Souris sediments around Denbigh. It interprets the former as probably linked to the Black Hills and the latter as apparently transported from the Canadian Shield.
overview.locator: North Dakota Notes 6, Ransom County and Lake Souris–Denbigh Deposit

history.text: In 1934, the University of North Dakota School of Mines conducted a federally assisted Gold Investigation around Denbigh. The survey account reports traces in some samples and describes small, rounded and flattened gold grains.
history.locator: North Dakota Notes 6, 1934 Gold Investigation and grain-description paragraphs
history.title: A systematic Denbigh investigation

places.text: The survey locates a historical gold deposit north of Fort Ransom in the Sheyenne River valley. It describes probably preglacial gravel, later buried by glaciers and exposed again by river erosion, associated with the Griswold Mine.
places.locator: North Dakota Notes 6, Ransom County
places.title: Sheyenne River: Fort Ransom area

places.text: The survey records gold in sand and gravel associated with glacial Lake Souris in McHenry, Bottineau and Pierce counties. Its Denbigh account links the material to glacial transport and subsequent meltwater sorting.
places.locator: North Dakota Notes 6, Lake Souris–Denbigh Deposit
places.title: Glacial Lake Souris: Denbigh area

researchNotes.locator: Recreational panning; claimant permission
researchNotes.title: BLM hand panning and claim rights
researchNotes.text: The BLM Montana–Dakotas packet says recreational hand-tool panning does not need a special BLM permit on eligible BLM land, but another person’s claim requires claimant permission. This agency-specific guidance does not identify an open stream, authorize private access or waive state requirements.

researchNotes.locator: Ransom County; Lake Souris–Denbigh; Bentley Lake; summary; modified August 31,2007
researchNotes.title: Fine grains and historical ventures
researchNotes.text: The Denbigh investigation found small rounded, flattened grains; Bentley Lake accounts describe flour gold. A largest-nugget anecdote is not a statewide typical size. NDGS describes failed short-lived historical ventures rather than a proven commercial field.

overview.text: Delaware Geological Survey places most of the state’s mineral localities in the northern Piedmont, with its gneisses and amphibolites. Coastal Plain occurrences reflect different depositional environments, including iron oxides and iron sulfides. This is geological background; a gold-bearing Delaware locality remains unverified in this Almanac.
overview.locator: Main text: Piedmont and Coastal Plain mineral settings

history.text: DGS describes Delaware’s Piedmont as eroded roots of the Appalachian mountain system. Its preserved mineralogy and structures chiefly record the Taconic mountain-building event; weathering continues to carry rock fragments into creeks and rivers.
history.locator: Main text: Taconic event and continuing erosion
history.title: The Piedmont’s exposed mountain roots

overview.text: KGS’s 1994 guide describes Kentucky’s predominantly sedimentary near-surface rocks as unfavorable for economic gold concentration. Its investigated samples had gold values within background ranges. This is a limited geological assessment, not proof of statewide absence or a verified recreational gold site.
overview.locator: Gold and Silver, printed pp. 49–50 / PDF pp. 31–32

history.text: The KGS guide identifies pyrite and muscovite mica as frequent sources of mistaken gold reports. Weathered mica can develop a brownish-gold color, so appearance alone is unreliable evidence of native gold.
history.locator: Gold and Silver, printed p. 49 / PDF p. 31
history.title: Minerals that can resemble gold

researchNotes.locator: Native Elements; Gold, Silver, Platinum; Kentucky rarity vs general gold settings
researchNotes.title: Rare gold and general mineralogy
researchNotes.text: KGS says native-element gold is not common in Kentucky. Its description of quartz veins, metamorphic rocks and placers is general mineralogy, not a list of proven Kentucky gold localities. No named gold stream is inferred from that discussion.

overview.text: South Carolina’s survey associates gold with the Piedmont northwest of the Fall Line. It describes deposits formed in volcanic rocks and gold released into stream sediments as crystalline bedrock erodes. Historical mining and minor stream finds document different parts of this mineral record.
overview.locator: Question 3: Where can gold be found in South Carolina?

facts.label: Historical gold production
facts.definition: Historical USGS statewide series, including early estimates.
facts.locator: State opening, printed p.231 / PDF p.237; Figure3; general estimate caveats, printed p.3

history.text: The state survey’s history records that Lardner Vanuxem’s 1825–26 geological survey reported gold in the then-named Spartanburg and Abbeville districts. This is an early documented survey report, not a claim about the state’s first discovery.
history.locator: History of the South Carolina Geological Survey: first two paragraphs
history.title: Gold in the early state survey

places.text: The survey’s Volume 35 study documents gold deposits at Haile in metamorphosed sedimentary and volcanic rocks of the Carolina slate belt. This geological occurrence record does not establish visitor or collecting permission.
places.locator: Haile article, printed p. 9 / PDF p. 13, abstract and introduction
places.title: Haile area, Lancaster County

places.text: A separate Volume 35 study describes hydrothermal gold mineralization in metamorphosed volcanic rocks at Brewer. It treats the deposit’s alteration and geochemistry; current operations and access require separate evidence.
places.locator: Brewer article, printed p. 37 / PDF p. 41, abstract
places.title: Brewer area near Jefferson

discovery.label: Early state-survey gold report
discovery.text: The South Carolina Geological Survey’s history records Lardner Vanuxem’s report of gold in the then-named Spartanburg and Abbeville districts. This is a dated survey record; the source does not settle the state’s first discovery.
discovery.locator: History of the South Carolina Geological Survey, Vanuxem paragraphs

researchNotes.locator: Question 3 gold in South Carolina; Question 2 mapping/publications
researchNotes.title: Geological maps and publications
researchNotes.text: SCGS offers a generalized statewide map, detailed quadrangle maps, drill-hole reports, bulletins and South Carolina Geology. Its gold FAQ points to Volume 35 on Carolina slate-belt deposits.

researchNotes.locator: Printed p. 232
researchNotes.title: Brewer and Haile ore minerals
researchNotes.text: PP610 describes pyrite-associated gold at Brewer and quartz/pyrite mineralization at Haile, including very fine gold. These are specific hard-rock ore descriptions; they do not establish the typical size in recreational stream finds.

researchNotes.locator: Printedpp 231–232
researchNotes.title: Placers before lode mining
researchNotes.text: USGS PP610 describes Haile placer discovery in 1827 and placer working at Brewer before 1830, followed by lode development. These establish localized historical placer mining; the present industrial mines and old property names are not recreational access.

overview.text: USGS documents the historical Coker Creek gold district in southern Monroe County. Mining focused on gold concentrated in weathered bedrock and alluvial material derived from gold-bearing rocks and a few quartz veins. This is historical occurrence evidence rather than a current access designation.
overview.locator: Metallic Resources: Gold, printed p. 18 / PDF p. 26

history.text: The 1982 USGS report describes Coker Creek’s main working period before the Civil War, followed by sporadic mining. It identifies the Annette Mining Company’s 1920s placer operation as a later serious attempt, within that report’s historical account.
history.locator: Metallic Resources: Gold, printed p. 18 / PDF p. 26
history.title: Coker Creek’s placer-mining history

places.text: USGS places the historic district around Coker Creek and several tributaries in southern Monroe County. The district-scale record does not identify an open stream reach or grant permission to collect.
places.locator: Metallic Resources: Gold, printed p. 18 / PDF p. 26
places.title: Coker Creek district
Coker Creek · Monroe County
places.text: The USGS report identifies Coker Creek and its tributaries as a historic gold-mining district.
places.locator: Metallic Resources: Gold, printed p. 18 / PDF p. 26

discovery.label: Coker Creek discovery
discovery.text: USGS dates the discovery of Coker Creek’s gold deposits in Monroe County to 1827. The district was most actively worked from that discovery through the Civil War. This regional date is not a verified statewide first-discovery claim.
discovery.locator: Metallic Resources: Gold, printed p. 18 / PDF p. 26

researchNotes.locator: Printed p. 240
researchNotes.title: A historical estimate for Coker Creek
researchNotes.text: USGS Professional Paper 610 cites a historical estimate of about 9,000 ounces from the Coker Creek area, attributed to a 1962 account. This is an approximate district figure, not a statewide total or an estimate of gold remaining.

researchNotes.locator: Printed p. 240
researchNotes.title: Ducktown’s sulfide ores
researchNotes.text: PP610 reports small gold/silver amounts in Ducktown primary and secondary sulfide ores, with pyrrhotite, chalcopyrite, pyrite and other minerals. Ducktown ore gold and Coker Creek placer gold are different evidence types.

overview.text: Virginia Energy documents gold mining from weathered near-surface lodes, veins, mineralized zones and placers. Most historic activity lay in the gold-pyrite belt, a northeast-trending belt extending from Fairfax County to southwestern Buckingham County. Additional prospects are scattered across the Piedmont and Blue Ridge.
overview.locator: Gold: final geological-setting paragraph

facts.label: Historical gold production
facts.definition: Historical USGS statewide series, including early estimates.
facts.locator: State opening, printed p.253 / PDF p.259; Figure3; general estimate caveats, printed p.3

history.text: Virginia Energy describes extensive early-nineteenth-century mining and a rapid decline as the California gold rush drew miners west. Smaller commercial efforts continued into the twentieth century.
history.title: Mining before and after the California rush

places.text: Virginia Energy identifies these counties among the largest concentrations of historic mines in the gold-pyrite belt. These county-scale records support mining history, while access to individual workings requires separate confirmation.
places.locator: Gold: largest concentrations of historical gold mines
places.title: Buckingham–Fluvanna–Louisa area

places.text: Also identified by Virginia Energy as counties with large concentrations of historical gold mines. A recorded mine or prospect is not an approved panning location.

Rappahannock River · below the falls
places.text: The survey’s account of Jefferson’s report places the ore on the river’s north side, about four miles below the falls; no precise coordinates are assigned.
places.locator: Gold Deposits: Historical, printed p. 26 / PDF p. 49

discovery.label: Earliest reference cited by the survey
discovery.text: Virginia Geological Survey’s Bulletin 47 identifies Jefferson’s 1782 account as the earliest accredited reference, describing gold-bearing ore near the Rappahannock River below the falls. This is a cited historical report, distinct from later commercial production.
discovery.locator: Gold Deposits: Historical, printed p. 26 / PDF p. 49

researchNotes.locator: Gold associations; gold-pyrite belt; first/last production fields; cumulative lower bound
researchNotes.title: Quartz and the gold-pyrite belt
researchNotes.text: Virginia Energy describes gold with quartz, pyrite and other sulfides, sometimes tellurides. Historic mining concentrated in the northeast-trending gold-pyrite belt and included lodes, veins, weathered zones and placers. The lode-mining map is not a public panning map.

overview.text: WVGES documents gold as an extremely low-abundance trace element in West Virginia coals. Its 2002 compilation reports detectable gold in a small subset of analyzed samples and describes probable tiny detrital particles. This laboratory evidence does not identify a recreational placer district.
overview.locator: Geologic Occurrence and Economic Impact; revised March 2, 2002

history.text: Most exposed West Virginia rocks are Paleozoic sedimentary deposits. WVGES describes relatively flat or gently folded rocks of the Appalachian Plateau in the west and folded, faulted rocks farther east, recording deposition, mountain building and erosion.
history.locator: Physiographic Provinces; General Stratigraphy and Structural Geology
history.title: The state’s sedimentary bedrock
